claims.text: Active learning focused near the phase boundary can reduce the computational cost of free-energy evaluations for both solid and fluid states.
A machine-learning interatomic potential can retain fidelity to vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration effects.
The elemental and binary systems proposed for initial validation have well-characterized fusion properties.
A potential trained on targeted ab initio data near the phase transition can replace explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD workflows.
Validation will span temperatures below and above the melting point.
Initial validation will use an elemental or binary system before extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Mirroring the conditions of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations will ensure fidelity.
The learned potential-energy surface will capture both solid- and fluid-phase behavior.
Targeted training will ensure that vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling contributions are retained.
Concentrating ab initio training data near the phase transition enables the model to learn the relevant free-energy landscape efficiently.
The surrogate potential can predict free energies otherwise obtained from long molecular-dynamics trajectories at a fraction of the computational cost.
The surrogate will reproduce solid–liquid free-energy differences with fidelity similar to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The surrogate will reproduce the fusion temperature with fidelity similar to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The surrogate will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The surrogate will outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Failure to capture all anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling effects could reduce accuracy when extending the method to high-entropy systems.
Al-Cu is a well-studied binary system suitable for the proposed benchmark.
